q: Your light turns green, but a pedestrian is still clearing the crosswalk. What should you do?
a: Wait until the pedestrian is safely clear
Proceed because green gives absolute right-of-way
why: A green light permits movement only after yielding to pedestrians and lawful traffic still in the intersection.

q: You approach a stale green light and the pedestrian signal shows DON'T WALK. What should you anticipate?
a: The light may turn yellow soon
The green light will remain indefinitely
Opposing traffic has a green arrow
why: A stale green may change soon; a DON'T WALK display is another cue to prepare to stop safely.

q: A green arrow and solid green light face you. What may drivers following the arrow do?
a: Use any lane regardless of markings
Proceed in the arrow direction without yielding to opposing traffic
why: The protected arrow movement may proceed, while all drivers must still avoid pedestrians or other lawful intersection users.

q: The lane-control signal above your lane changes from a green arrow to a red X. What should you do?
a: Move safely into a lane displaying a green arrow
why: A red X means do not enter or remain in that lane because it may serve oncoming traffic.

q: Yellow lights flash on a pedestrian-crossing sign, but no one has stepped onto the road yet. What is required?
a: Reduce to no more than 30 km/h and be ready to yield or stop
why: Flashing yellow pedestrian-crossing lights require a maximum of 30 km/h and yielding or stopping for pedestrians.

q: At 4:20 p.m. on a school day, you enter a school zone with no special times posted. Is the zone active?
a: Yes, the default afternoon period ends at 4:30 p.m.
why: The provincial default afternoon school-zone period is 3:00-4:30 p.m. on school days.

q: You enter a playground zone 30 minutes after sunset with no different times posted. Is the restriction active?
a: Yes, until one hour after sunset
why: Default playground-zone restrictions remain active until one hour after sunset every day.

q: How do you know a school or playground zone has ended?
a: A sign shows a higher speed or the end of the zone
why: Continue observing the zone limit until a higher maximum or end-of-zone sign appears.

q: After parallel parking, your wheels are 70 cm from the curb. What should you do?
a: Reposition within 50 cm of the curb
Leave the vehicle because it is under one metre
why: A parallel-parked vehicle's wheels must be no more than 50 cm from the curb.

q: You signal left to leave a parallel space, but a cyclist is approaching in your blind spot. What should you do?
a: Wait for the cyclist to pass
Pull out before the cyclist arrives
Open the door to warn the cyclist
why: A signal does not grant right-of-way; shoulder-check and wait until traffic and cyclists are clear.

q: When entering an angle space, your vehicle is not centred by the midpoint of the stall. What is safest?
a: Ignore the position if the front fits
Correct slowly while checking both sides
why: Move slowly, centre the vehicle, and monitor clearance from vehicles on both sides.

q: While reversing from an angle stall, the rear of your vehicle becomes even with a longer vehicle beside you. What should you do?
a: Rely only on the backup camera
Stop and check for traffic and pedestrians before continuing
why: Stop at the point where you can begin checking beyond the obstructing vehicle, then continue cautiously.

q: A backup camera shows a clear path, but you have not looked behind the vehicle. May you reverse?
a: No, look around and in the direction of travel before reversing
Yes, the camera replaces all checks
why: Cameras assist but do not replace a complete check around the vehicle and looking in the direction of travel.

q: While reversing right, which way does the front of your vehicle swing?
why: The front swings opposite the direction the rear is moving, creating a hazard that must also be checked.

q: You are backing from a stall while another vehicle drives along the aisle. Who should yield?
a: You, because you are entering the aisle
The aisle vehicle, because you began moving
why: A vehicle backing from a parking space must yield to traffic and pedestrians already using the aisle.

q: A stop line is several metres before the crosswalk. Where must you make the required stop?
a: At the edge of the intersecting road
why: When a stop line exists, stop before it; move forward cautiously afterward only if needed for visibility.

q: Two vehicles reach a four-way stop together. You are on the left. Who normally proceeds first?
a: You, because you are turning left
why: At simultaneous arrivals, courtesy allows the vehicle on the right to proceed first.

q: A parked van blocks your view at an uncontrolled intersection. How should you approach?
a: Drive partly into the intersection before slowing
Slow enough to stop easily and check both directions
Maintain speed because traffic on the right must yield
why: Adjust speed for limited visibility and be able to stop before a conflict develops.

q: Leaving a driveway, you cross a sidewalk before reaching the street. What is the correct sequence?
a: Stop before the sidewalk, yield to pedestrians, then stop or yield before entering the street
Cross the sidewalk first, then stop
why: Stop before the sidewalk crossing and yield to pedestrians before entering the main roadway.

q: Your light is green, but traffic leaves no room beyond the crosswalk. What should you do?
a: Enter and stop in the crosswalk
why: Do not enter until you can completely clear the intersection and far crosswalk.

q: You approach a roundabout in the right lane but want an exit beyond the first. What is safest?
a: Change to the correct approach lane before entering if safe
Enter right and change lanes inside
Stop in the circle to reposition
why: Choose the correct lane before entry and never change lanes within the circular intersection.

q: The vehicle beside you swings wide during a dual turn. What should you do?
a: Stop in the middle of the turn
Maintain your lane and be prepared to avoid a collision
why: Stay in the corresponding lane, watch adjacent traffic, and take safe evasive action if necessary.

q: You are waiting to turn left and an oncoming motorcycle appears farther away than it is. What should guide your decision?
a: Rely on the driver behind you
Wait unless there is clearly enough time and space
Assume its small size means it is slow
why: Motorcycle size makes speed and distance difficult to judge; turn only with a clearly safe gap.

q: Your mirrors appear clear before a highway lane change. What final check is still required?
a: A glance at the fuel gauge
A shoulder check of the blind spot
why: Mirrors do not show every blind spot; shoulder-check immediately before moving laterally.

q: Traffic on the freeway is moving at 100 km/h while you travel at 60 km/h in the acceleration lane. What should you do?
a: Accelerate toward traffic speed and select a safe gap
Stop at the end of the lane
Use the shoulder until traffic clears
why: Use the acceleration lane to approach the speed of freeway traffic before merging into a safe opening.

q: Another vehicle is entering the freeway beside you. Who has priority?
a: Traffic already on the freeway, though it should cooperate when safe
Whichever vehicle is ahead by one metre
why: Entering drivers must yield to freeway traffic; drivers on the freeway should adjust safely when possible.

q: You miss your freeway exit. What should you do?
why: Never stop, reverse, or cross the gore; continue safely to the next exit.

q: A vehicle begins passing you on a two-lane highway. What should you do?
a: Maintain a steady speed and allow the pass
why: Do not accelerate while being passed; maintain a predictable speed and provide room.

q: You are passing and realize an oncoming vehicle is closer than expected. What is the safest priority?
a: Abandon the pass and return safely if possible
Exceed the speed limit by any amount
Force the passed vehicle onto the shoulder
why: If the pass cannot be completed safely and legally, reduce speed and return behind the vehicle when possible.

q: Rain begins during highway driving. How should your following distance change?
a: Match the distance used in dry weather
why: Wet conditions increase stopping distance and require a larger space cushion.

q: A line of vehicles forms behind you on a rural highway. What should you do when possible?
a: Brake to make them back away
Use a safe turnout or stop off-road to let them pass
why: Allow faster traffic to pass from a safe off-road location when a queue develops behind you.

q: Your ABS activates during an emergency stop and the pedal vibrates. What should you do?
a: Keep firm continuous pressure and steer where needed
why: ABS pedal vibration is normal; maintain firm pressure and continue steering.

q: Your brake pedal suddenly goes to the floor. What should you try first?
a: Pump the brake pedal to build pressure
Shift into Park at highway speed
why: Pumping may restore hydraulic pressure; then reduce speed and use other safe stopping methods.

q: A front tire blows out at highway speed. What should you avoid?
why: Abrupt braking or steering can cause loss of control after a blowout.

q: Power steering fails while the vehicle is moving. What should you expect?
a: Steering will require much more effort
The steering wheel will turn itself
why: Manual steering remains possible but requires significantly more force; slow and stop safely.

q: Both headlights fail at night. What should you do?
a: Use only hazard lights to keep driving
Try other light settings, slow, and move safely off the road
why: Attempt to restore lighting, reduce speed, and leave the roadway safely as soon as possible.

q: Your vehicle begins a braking skid without ABS. What should you do to regain steering?
a: Ease brake pressure enough for the wheels to roll
Press harder until all wheels lock
Turn sharply away from your path
why: Locked wheels cannot steer; reduce pressure enough to restore rolling traction.

q: You enter a slippery curve too quickly and the vehicle slides outward. Where should you look?
a: Toward the path you want to follow
why: Look and steer toward the intended path while making smooth corrections.

q: The steering suddenly feels light in heavy rain. What is the safest response?
a: Accelerate to push through the water
Ease off the accelerator and avoid abrupt braking or steering
why: These are signs of hydroplaning; slow gradually and keep steering inputs smooth.

q: A deer appears ahead and a vehicle is approaching in the opposite lane. What is your safest priority?
a: Close your eyes and sound the horn
Brake firmly while maintaining control in your lane
why: A controlled stop is generally safer than swerving into oncoming traffic or another fixed hazard.

q: After a minor collision, vehicles can move and no one is injured. What should drivers do?
a: Move to a safe location out of traffic and exchange information
why: When safe and lawful, clear traffic, exchange required information, and follow collision-reporting requirements.

q: A pedestrian waits at an unmarked crosswalk at an intersection. What should you do?
a: Pass a stopped vehicle beside the crosswalk
Yield and allow the pedestrian to cross safely
Proceed because only marked crosswalks count
why: Intersections contain marked or unmarked crosswalks where drivers must yield to pedestrians.

q: A cyclist moves left within the lane to avoid debris. What should you do?
a: Slow and give the cyclist space
Pass closely before the cyclist moves farther
why: Cyclists may need lateral room to avoid hazards; wait for a safe passing opportunity.

q: A motorcycle's turn signal remains flashing after an intersection. What should you assume?
a: The rider must turn at the next road
It is safe to pull out
Do not assume it will turn; wait for the rider's action
why: Motorcycle signals may not cancel automatically; rely on observed movement, not the signal alone.

q: A large truck signals right but first moves left. What is it likely doing?
a: Setting up for a wide right turn
Inviting you to pass on the right
Changing permanently to the left lane
why: Large vehicles may swing left to complete a right turn; never enter the space beside them.

q: You are beside a truck on a downhill grade. Why should you avoid lingering there?
a: Your vehicle will use more fuel
The truck has large blind spots and may need extra room
why: Stay visible and avoid large-vehicle blind spots, especially where braking and lane control are demanding.

q: A school bus's alternating amber lights begin flashing. What should you prepare to do?
a: Stop only if children are visible
Slow and prepare to stop because the red lights may follow
Pass before the red lights activate
why: Amber school-bus lights warn that the bus is preparing to stop and activate its red lights.

q: An emergency vehicle approaches from behind while you are in an intersection. What should you do?
a: Clear the intersection safely, then move right and stop
why: Do not block the intersection; clear it safely, then pull right and stop for the emergency vehicle.

q: A snowplow creates a cloud that blocks your view. What should you do?
a: Stay well back and do not pass until visibility and conditions are safe
Follow closely to see its lights
why: Snowplows can create severe whiteout conditions and may operate in formation; keep a large following distance.

q: A train clears one track at a multiple-track crossing, but the gate remains down. What should you do?
a: Wait; another train may be approaching and the signals still control
why: Remain stopped until gates rise and signals stop; a second train may be approaching on another track.
